<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with disciplined, closed-book reasoning and no fake sourcing. PRO built a clean core: irreversibility plus reversed burden of proof, culminating in a genuinely strong default comparison (uncertainty means no access vs. uncertainty means the market) and a memorable close. CON, however, identified and sustained the two hardest structural burdens and kept converting them into comparison rather than restatement. First, "name the finding": PRO eventually produced a statutory test (demonstrate evaluations run, thresholds met, monitoring in place; refusal for failure to demonstrate), but CON's reply that this is a mandated evaluation-and-publication duty rather than a licence — the licence adding only a state stamp, plus a compliance defence that shifts liability toward the authority — materially shrank the marginal value of PRO's instrument. Second, the extraterritoriality turn: CON used PRO's own irreversibility premise against it, and the GDPR flip (PRO's best cross-border analogy is a conduct-based, not entry-based, regime) was the sharpest single move of the debate. PRO's chokepoint answer (hospitals, banks, ministries, cloud, app stores) was its best counter and was only partially neutralised, which keeps PRO's route alive but narrower. CON's textual pressure on "move from" also forced PRO to concede that use-level duties survive intact, leaving PRO defending risk-based-plus-a-gate; PRO's answer (scope was pre-committed in the opening; background law survives in every licensed sector) was consistent and reasonable, so CON only banked partial value there. Pressure Questions favoured CON: the yes/no trap and the "name the statutory test / would a court uphold refusal" question both exposed real burdens, and PRO answered them squarely with proper A1:/A2: labels, which limited the damage but did not erase it. PRO's questions were fair but more argumentative than probing. Net: CON reduced PRO's gate to "a stamp, not a stop" against the models PRO fears most, and made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's turn on PRO's own analogy and premise: GDPR reaches across borders precisely because it attaches duties to conduct rather than to market entry, and if weights proliferate permanently then an EU permission slip is structurally incapable of stopping the models PRO fears — crystallised in the closing's "Refuse whose entry? That file never files an application."</best_rebuttal>
